title: J'accuse!
byline: Dir. Abel Gance; prod. Pathé Frères (France, 1919). US theatrical release October 1921 as 'I Accuse' via United Artists.

evidence.note: First published France, April 1919. Any US copyright on a 1919 work carries a maximum 95-year term expiring January 1, 2015. Published before 1930, so firmly within the pre-1930 bright line for US public domain by term as of 2026.
evidence.source: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain — Public Domain Day 2025

evidence.note: J'accuse! is a French work (Pathé/Gance). France is a URAA-eligible WTO member. Abel Gance died November 10, 1981; the work was still protected under French law on January 1, 1996 (French term: 70 years pma, running to approximately 2051). Under 17 U.S.C. § 104A, URAA would have restored US copyright effective January 1, 1996. However, the maximum restored term — the remainder of the 95-year US copyright term calculated from first publication in 1919 — expired January 1, 2015. The print is PD in the US by exhaustion of that URAA-restored term.
evidence.source: U.S. Copyright Office Circular 38b — URAA and Copyright Restoration

evidence.note: J'accuse! (1919) is a silent film; no recorded score accompanies the original print, and that print is PD. Commercial and restoration releases uniformly add modern scores, each of which is an independently protected sound recording. The 2018 Flicker Alley release pairs the restored print with composer Robert Israel's newly commissioned symphonic score. That audio track is not cleared by the print's PD status.
evidence.source: Flicker Alley — J'Accuse: A Film by Abel Gance (product page)

evidence.note: Original scenario written by Abel Gance; no prior novel, play, or other literary work underlies the film. The screenplay was created as part of the 1919 production and shares its publication date. Maximum 95-year US copyright term expired January 1, 2015.
evidence.source: U.S. Copyright Office — Duration of Copyright (Circular 15a)

evidence.note: A 2007 restoration by Nederlands Filmmuseum and Lobster Films assembled elements from six surviving prints; Flicker Alley released a reconstruction on November 20, 2018 with Robert Israel's new symphonic score. Both versions incorporate protected editorial decisions and/or new recorded-score elements that are not cleared by the underlying film's PD status.
evidence.source: San Francisco Silent Film Festival — J'Accuse program notes

editorial:
J'accuse! is the 1919 French anti-war silent film written and directed by Abel Gance, produced by Pathé Frères and starring Romuald Joubé as pacifist poet Jean Diaz. Filmed partly within active military zones during the final year of World War I, its climactic 'return of the dead' sequence used actual French soldiers on leave from Verdun — many of whom were killed before the film reached screens. United Artists distributed a heavily re-edited American version titled 'I Accuse' in October 1921, excising Gance's antiwar message and grafting on a patriotic resolution. The original 1919 print was reassembled in 2007 by Nederlands Filmmuseum and Lobster Films from six archival copies.

The original print is in the US public domain: first published in France in 1919, any domestic US copyright term expired by January 1, 2015, and even accounting for URAA restoration (Gance died 1981; France protected the work well past January 1, 1996), the URAA-extended term ran to the same 95-year ceiling and is likewise exhausted. The practical rights trap is the score. J'accuse! is a silent film, which means every commercial copy on the market carries a modern soundtrack that is its own protected work. The 2018 Flicker Alley release uses Robert Israel's new symphonic score; that audio track cannot be reproduced. Reusers should pull from the unscored print on the Internet Archive and supply their own music or commission silence.
faq: Can I use footage from the Flicker Alley Blu-ray in my documentary?

The visual content is public domain, but the Flicker Alley disc pairs it with Robert Israel's 2018 symphonic score, which is a protected sound recording. You can use the visuals only if you mute or replace the audio entirely. For a fully unencumbered source, use the unscored print at archive.org/details/silent-jaccuse.
Is there an underlying novel or play I need to license?

No. Abel Gance wrote an original scenario; J'accuse! was not adapted from any pre-existing novel, play, or short story. There is no underlying literary work to clear. The screenplay and story expired under the same 95-year US copyright term as the film itself.
